cases.C27: Anchorite Labs is distinctive rather than generic: its chosen enclosure neatly signals bounded agency; “Labs” makes the monastic wit practical, with clear UK registration and usable domains.
cases.C16: Imprimatur signals rigorous sign-off, not censorship; UK Companies House and all key domains are clear, unlike vague 'shield' rivals.
cases.C18: Redoubt's defensive imagery nails contained-agent architecture; domain gaps and niche associations are solvable branding issues, not fatal flaws.
cases.C29: Palantir proved literary archaisms work; 'Seneschal' perfectly embodies our delegated-authority thesis, while pristine domain availability and Companies House clearance outweigh minor spelling hurdles with regulated, enterprise buyers.
cases.C23: Penstock Labs precisely evokes metered, controlled flow—capability and information passing only when granted. The Pentera sound-alike risk is limited; Companies House is clear, domains are available, and its sober engineering metaphor suits CISO buyers.
cases.C22: Labs separates it from Bailiwick.com; jurisdictional authority is exactly the governance story. Jersey/Guernsey tint is faint beside a precise, CISO-legible architecture metaphor.
cases.C15: Military tone? Zero-trust itself descends from military command doctrine. 'Countermand' names the exact human veto your architecture sells—instantly memorable, unambiguously ownable, sober where CISOs measure sobriety.
cases.C11: Distinct spelling, unrelated sector from funded Cautio. Latin 'cautio' means legal guarantee, richer than mere caution. Pronounce COH-shee-ah; .co.uk and .io free, Companies House clear.
cases.C25: Runnymede Trust is a think tank, not a tech firm; "Labs" signals product R&D. Magna Carta metaphor is exact for "architecture of distrust": agents granted limited, documented authority under rule of law. UK gravitas reassures
cases.C17: No core TLDs free, but .app/.dev/.tech available; precise medieval term for delegated, revocable authority mirrors thesis perfectly. Obscurity avoids AI clichés; pronunciation settles instantly. Tiny US consultancies pose zero market confusion.
cases.C26: Chary Labs perfectly mirrors the core ‘least‑privilege’ stance: ‘chary’ literally means cautious, signalling deliberate gate‑keeping. The name is unique, domain‑available, and avoids any existing AI‑security trademarks.
cases.C31: Vallum Labs invokes fortified boundaries—ramparts and controlled gates—directly resonating with the architecture of distrust. Despite a few nearby uses, the name remains distinctive and domain‑ready.
cases.C24: The architectural weight of Claustra pivots the risk of 'claustrophobia' into a promise of airtight control—precisely the rigorous boundary-setting demanded by CISOs in regulated sectors.
cases.C30: The institutional gravity is a strategic asset; it signals the governance, maturity, and delegated authority necessary to gain trust from enterprise CFOs and COOs in regulated markets.
cases.C12: Veto.so precedent is real but operates in different market (runtime auth for agents vs. enterprise AI workflows). Memorable, Latin-grounded, perfectly captures human override. Domain availability strong.
cases.C14: Vouchsafe.id is biometric identity; this is AI governance—distinct enough. Archaic language is intentional differentiator for serious buyers. Domains available. Harder to say is feature, not bug, for gravitas.
